tutorial.title: Welcome to Vestige
tutorial.intro: This is a complete guide to Vestige — what it does, how it works, and why it's built the way it is. No programming background needed. If you can use Instagram, you can understand Vestige.

whatIs.title: What is Vestige?
whatIs.p1: Vestige is a memory system for AI assistants. Think of it as a second brain — it remembers things so your AI doesn't have to start from scratch every conversation. When you chat with your AI tomorrow, it'll remember what you talked about today.
whatIs.p2: But it's not a simple notepad. Your brain naturally forgets things over time — and that's actually useful, because it keeps the important stuff front and center. Vestige works the same way: memories you use often stay strong, while stuff you never touch slowly fades into the background.
whatIs.p3: This isn't science fiction. Vestige is built on real neuroscience research from the last 50 years — the same principles scientists use to understand how human memory works. It just applies them to AI.

library.title: A Smart Library
library.desc: Imagine a library where the books you read most often automatically move to the front shelf, and books nobody touches slowly drift to the back. That's how Vestige manages memories — the useful ones are always within reach.

brain.title: Your Brain, But for AI
brain.desc: When you sleep, your brain replays the day's events and decides what to keep. Vestige has a "Dream Cycle" that does the same thing — it finds connections, spots contradictions, and strengthens what matters.

web.title: A Web of Connected Ideas
web.desc: In your head, thinking about "pizza" might remind you of Italy, which reminds you of that trip, which reminds you of your friend Marco. Vestige connects memories the same way — through meaning, not just keywords.

howMemoryWorks.title: How a memory lives and dies
howMemoryWorks.subtitle: The lifecycle of a single memory, from creation to potential forgetting

s1.title: Birth — Your AI saves something
s1.desc: When your AI learns something important (a bug fix, a decision, a person's name), it sends it to Vestige. Vestige analyzes it, figures out what it means, and stores it with full strength.

s2.title: Connection — Finding related memories
s2.desc: Vestige doesn't just file it away. It converts the text into a mathematical representation (called an embedding) and uses it to find memories with similar meaning. These get linked together automatically.

s3.title: Strengthening — Every time it's used
s3.desc: Each time your AI searches for this memory and finds it, the memory gets stronger. This is called the Testing Effect — recalling something makes it easier to recall next time. It's the same reason flashcards work.

s4.title: Decay — The forgetting curve
s4.desc: If nobody accesses this memory for weeks, it starts to fade. This follows a mathematical formula called a power law — fast at first, then slower. Well-learned memories (high stability) fade much slower than new ones.

s5.title: Revival or Fade — Your choice
s5.desc: You can manually "Strengthen" a fading memory from the dashboard, or let it continue to decline. If it drops below a threshold, it becomes a candidate for cleanup. Nothing is deleted automatically — you're always in control.

retention.title: Retention
retention.desc: A percentage showing how well a memory is remembered right now. 100% means perfectly fresh, 0% means almost forgotten. Every time you retrieve a memory, its retention jumps back up. Ignore it and it slowly drops.

dualStrength.title: Dual Strength
dualStrength.desc: Each memory has two strengths: Storage (how deeply it's encoded — like how well you learned it) and Retrieval (how easily it comes to mind right now). A memory can be deeply learned but temporarily hard to recall — like a word on the tip of your tongue.

dream.title: Dream Cycle
dream.desc: Just like your brain processes memories during sleep, Vestige has a "dream" mode. It replays recent memories, finds surprising connections between them, spots contradictions (did you save two conflicting things?), and generates insights.

connections.title: Connections (Spreading Activation)
connections.desc: Memories link to each other through meaning. When you search for one memory, related ones light up too — like a chain reaction. This is based on the ACT-R model from cognitive science (John Anderson, Carnegie Mellon).

decay.title: Natural Decay (Forgetting Curve)
decay.desc: Memories lose strength over time if not used. This follows Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, discovered in 1885. It's not a bug — it's a feature. By letting unimportant memories fade, the system stays clean and the important stuff stands out.

types.title: Memory Types
types.desc: Each memory is classified: Fact (something objectively true), Concept (an abstract idea), Event (something that happened at a specific time), Person, Place, Note, Pattern (a recurring theme), or Decision (a choice that was made and why).

intentions.title: Reminders (Prospective Memory)
intentions.desc: You can set triggers for the future: "remind me when we talk about databases" (context trigger) or "remind me next Friday" (time trigger). This is based on prospective memory research — the psychology of remembering to remember.

search.title: Hybrid Search
search.desc: Vestige doesn't just match keywords. It combines three methods: exact text matching (BM25), meaning-based search (embeddings), and a reranker that picks the best results. It's like having Google, a librarian, and a fact-checker working together.

reflect.title: Self-Reflection
reflect.desc: A metacognitive tool that analyzes your memories for problems: contradictions (you saved conflicting info), knowledge gaps (topics you know little about), stale decisions (choices made months ago that might need revisiting), and hidden patterns.

confidence.title: Confidence Scoring
confidence.desc: Not all memories are equally trustworthy. "Python 3.12 was released in October 2023" is a hard fact. "I think we should use Redis" is an opinion. Vestige scores confidence on multiple dimensions so you know what to trust.

science.title: The Science Behind Vestige
science.p1: Vestige draws on peer-reviewed memory research, but we are careful about what we actually re-prove vs. what we just borrow. The forgetting curve follows the FSRS-6 algorithm, which is open-source and benchmarked against SM-2 by the FSRS team — Vestige neither retrains nor re-benchmarks it. The dual-strength model comes from Bjork & Bjork (1992), who showed that storage and retrieval are independent dimensions of memory.
science.p2: The connection system is a spreading-activation walk on the memory graph — the lineage is Collins & Loftus (1975) semantic-network theory rather than the full ACT-R activation equation. The dream cycle is inspired by hippocampal replay during sleep, where consolidation strengthens important pathways and prunes weak ones; what runs inside Vestige is a four-phase batch heuristic that mimics that loop, not a biophysical model.
science.p3: When Vestige flags an opinion as low-confidence it is doing a retention-based consistency check, not Tetlock-style superforecaster calibration — the system has no ground-truth signal to score predictions against, so it compares how strongly opinions are held relative to facts on the same topic. The goal is the same as Kahneman wrote about: a system that doesn't just remember, but flags when its own beliefs need a second look.

graph.title: Graph
graph.desc: A 3D map of all your memories. Each glowing dot is a memory, and the lines between them show connections. Bigger dots have higher retention. The colors indicate the type (blue for facts, purple for concepts, yellow for events). The graph continuously moves using force simulation — related memories attract each other.
graph.tip: Click any node to see its full content, retention stats, and connections. Scroll to zoom. The graph adapts to your color theme.

memories.title: Memories
memories.desc: A searchable list of everything Vestige remembers. You can filter by type (facts, decisions, people…) or search by keywords. Click any memory to see its full details: retention percentage, storage and retrieval strengths, a forecast curve showing how retention will change over time, creation date, and all tags.
memories.tip: Use "Strengthen" on memories you want to keep. Use "Weaken" on outdated information. You can also delete memories permanently or click "Explore connections" to see what's linked.

timeline.title: Timeline
timeline.desc: A calendar view showing when memories were created. Pick any day to see what was saved. This is useful when you're thinking "I remember my AI learned something about that last week" — just find the day and browse.

feed.title: Activity
feed.desc: A real-time stream of everything happening in Vestige: new memories being saved, searches being performed, dream cycles running, connections being discovered, retention decay being applied. Each event is color-coded. Think of it as a heartbeat monitor for your memory system.

explore.title: Explore
explore.desc: The detective tool. Three modes: Associations (what's directly connected to a memory), Chains (the shortest path between two memories — like Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon), and Bridges (surprising connections between distant ideas that you didn't expect). This uses the spreading activation network under the hood.
explore.tip: Try Bridges mode with two unrelated memories — the bridging concepts it finds can spark real insights.

intentions.title: Reminders
intentions.desc: Set up future triggers. A context trigger fires when a topic comes up ("when we discuss authentication, remind me about the security audit"). A time trigger fires on a date. You can set priority (high/medium/low) and deadlines. Fulfilled reminders move to the archive.

stats.title: Overview
stats.desc: Your memory dashboard in numbers: total memories, average retention, retention distribution histogram (how many memories are in each strength bracket), type breakdown (how many facts vs. events vs. decisions), and a list of endangered memories that are fading and might need your attention.

settings.title: Settings
settings.desc: The control room. System information (version, embedding model, connection status), maintenance operations (Dream Cycle, Consolidation), metacognitive tools (Self-Reflection, Confidence Audit), the search pipeline visualization, and memory governance (retention distribution, endangered memories).
settings.tip: Run a Dream Cycle after a busy week. Run Self-Reflection when you want to spot contradictions or stale decisions in your knowledge base.

briefing.title: Briefing
briefing.desc: Your morning dashboard. Automatic Reflection highlights contradictions and gaps; Doubt mode surfaces low-confidence memories you can verify or weaken; Dream remains a deliberate heavier action for finding new connections.
briefing.tip: Start here for "what needs attention today" before diving into lists or the graph.

review.title: Review
review.desc: Spaced-repetition queue for memories that FSRS schedules for recall today. Quick rating (Again / Hard / Good / Easy) tunes the next interval and keeps important knowledge from fading.

hubs.title: Topic Hubs
hubs.desc: Clusters of related memories the Dream Cycle stitches into one card: shared topic, member count, and the timestamp of the last refresh. A high-level map of what the engine has already grouped.
hubs.tip: Open a hub when you want a topic-level overview without clicking every memory one by one.

insights.title: Insights
insights.desc: Machine-generated observations from dream runs and reflections. They stay tentative until you Promote them — that's the validation step. Filters separate validated from pending so you can focus on what still needs a call.
insights.tip: Treat insights as hypotheses to triage, not as ground truth.

decisions.title: Decisions
decisions.desc: A read-only gallery of structured choices the agent recorded: alternatives, weighted scores, recommendation, and validity dates. Filter by active vs expired to see what still governs behaviour and what has been superseded.
decisions.tip: Use this view to find the rationale behind a past choice. Editing happens on the MCP side so the audit trail stays consistent.

temporal.title: Temporal
temporal.desc: Time-scoped facts: which versions are currently valid, which have expired, and the full history of a topic across edits. Invalidate a memory when a newer fact replaces it — the engine writes valid_until to now() and demotes the row so search stops surfacing the old version.
temporal.tip: History mode needs a topic — the engine scopes versions to the subject line you pick.

reasoning.title: Reasoning
reasoning.desc: The deep_reference engine answering a question with full provenance: evidence memories, contradictions it found, superseded rows, and the topic's evolution timeline. FSRS-6 trust scoring weighs the evidence so the highest-retention memories rank first.
reasoning.tip: Use this when you need not just an answer but the audit trail behind it — useful for verifying a claim before promoting an Insight.

howTo.title: How do I actually use this?
howTo.p1: Vestige runs as a background service for your AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, etc.). You don't type memories in manually — your AI saves them automatically during conversations. This dashboard is your window into what's been stored. Here's a good routine:
howTo.li1: Open the Graph once a week to get a big-picture view of your knowledge. See if there are clusters you didn't expect.
howTo.li2: Use Memories when you need to find something specific, clean up outdated info, or strengthen important knowledge.
howTo.li3: Check Overview when you have a few minutes — see which memories are fading and decide if they're worth keeping.
howTo.li4: Run a Dream Cycle from Settings every week or two. It's like letting your AI sleep on what it's learned.

faq.q1: Can Vestige delete my memories without asking?
faq.a1: No. Vestige never deletes anything on its own. Memories can fade (retention drops), but the row stays in the database. Only you delete memories — manually from the Memories page or the Graph detail panel, or by running garbage collection explicitly in Settings (and even there a dry-run shows you what would go before anything is removed).
faq.q2: What happens if Vestige goes offline?
faq.a2: Your AI continues working normally — it just won't have long-term memory until Vestige is back. All your stored memories are safe in a local SQLite database on your machine. Nothing is lost.
faq.a3: Once running, no — everything happens locally. The embedding model (nomic-embed-text-v1.5) runs on your CPU via ONNX/fastembed, the database is a local SQLite file, and the reranker (Jina v2) also runs locally. The single exception is the first launch: the embedding and reranker weights are downloaded from Hugging Face the first time you start the server (they are cached on disk after that). At runtime: no API calls, no cloud, no telemetry.
faq.q4: What's the difference between Dream and Consolidation?
faq.a4: Dream Cycle is creative — it replays memories, finds connections, spots contradictions, and generates insights. Think of it as sleep. Consolidation is maintenance — it applies decay, generates missing embeddings, merges duplicates, and computes activation scores. Think of it as housekeeping.
faq.q5: Why do some memories fade faster than others?
faq.a5: Two reasons: stability and usage. A memory with high stability (well-learned, reviewed multiple times) fades slowly — it might take months. A memory with low stability (new, never reviewed) fades in days. The math follows the FSRS-6 power law forgetting curve.
faq.a6: An embedding is a list of 384 numbers that captures the meaning of a piece of text. Similar texts have similar numbers. This lets Vestige find memories by meaning, not just by keywords. "How do I deploy to production?" and "What's the deployment process?" would have very similar embeddings, even though they share few words.
faq.q7: Can I use Vestige without AI? Just as a personal knowledge base?
faq.a7: Technically yes — you can add memories via the MCP protocol from any compatible client. But Vestige is designed to work best as a background companion for AI assistants that automatically save and retrieve relevant context.
faq.a8: Model Context Protocol — an open standard by Anthropic that lets AI assistants communicate with external tools. Vestige implements MCP so any compatible AI (Claude, Cursor, etc.) can read and write memories through a standard interface.

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.retention: The probability of successfully recalling a memory right now (0-100%). Decays over time, resets on successful retrieval.
glossary.storage: How deeply a memory is encoded. Increases with every retrieval. High storage means the memory is durable — it won't fade easily.
glossary.retrieval: How easily a memory comes to mind right now. Drops over time, resets to 100% when you access the memory.
glossary.fsrs: Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler (version 6). The algorithm that estimates when a memory will fade and when it should be reviewed. The FSRS team's open SRS benchmark compares it against SM-2; Vestige uses their default weights as-is.
glossary.embedding: A vector of 384 numbers that represents the meaning of a text. Generated by the nomic-embed-text-v1.5 model running locally on your machine.
glossary.dream: A neuroscience-inspired process that replays memories, finds connections between them, detects contradictions, and generates insights. Based on hippocampal replay during sleep.
glossary.activation: When you think about one thing, related things come to mind. In Vestige, accessing one memory "activates" linked memories via a bounded walk on the memory graph — semantic-network style (Collins & Loftus, 1975) rather than the full ACT-R activation equation.
glossary.consolidation: Routine maintenance: apply forgetting curve decay, generate missing embeddings, merge duplicate memories, compute activation scores.
glossary.nodeType: The category of a memory: fact, concept, event, person, place, note, pattern, or decision. Determines how the memory appears on the graph.
glossary.mcp: Model Context Protocol — the communication standard that lets AI assistants read from and write to Vestige.

tutorial.footer: That's everything. Explore the pages at your own pace. Vestige handles the complexity — you just need to look around and occasionally run a Dream Cycle.

live.subtitle: Picked live from your database. Abstract decay numbers, made concrete.
live.explainer: Retention sits at {{retention}}% after {{days}} days. Every search that finds this memory bumps it back up; weeks of silence let it drift down.

empty.subtitle: Nothing to show yet
empty.body: Once your AI saves a few memories, this card will pick one and visualise its retention. Until then, the Briefing page is the best starting point.

quiz.title: Quick check (4 questions)
quiz.subtitle: Make sure the load-bearing ideas landed. Wrong answers come with a short hint.
quiz.scoreReview: Re-skim the highlighted sections and try again.

q1.opt0: How many memories Vestige currently stores
q1.opt1: Disk space the memory file consumes
q1.opt2: The chance the engine can recall a memory right now
q1.opt3: How many tags the memory has been given
q1.hint: Retention is an FSRS-6 probability score (0–100%) that resets when the memory is retrieved and drops while it sits unused.

q2.prompt: When does Vestige delete a memory on its own?
q2.opt1: Never — deletion always needs your confirmation
q2.hint: Memories fade but stay in the database. Garbage collection marks candidates; you have the final word.

q3.prompt: Which page surfaces memories the engine is least sure about?
q3.hint: Doubt mode on the Briefing page ranks memories by low confidence so you can verify or weaken them.

q4.prompt: What does a Dream Cycle do?
q4.opt0: Deletes the oldest memories without warning
q4.opt3: Replays memories, finds connections, spots contradictions
q4.hint: Dream is the creative pass. Consolidation is the housekeeping pass. Different jobs.
